<meta>continues from previous page: ...as there is no other purpose.</meta>

Thus, indeed, the Supreme is taught as being beyond all these, so it is reasonable; it is not the case that superiority is taught for each of them individually. Why? Because there is no purpose. For no purpose is seen or heard when superiority is understood in the others. However, when the Person <term>puruṣa</term> is understood as being beyond the senses and so on, and beyond the totality of all objects, a purpose is seen: the attainment of liberation <term>mokṣa</term>. And so the Shruti says, "Having realized this, one is liberated from the mouth of death" (Katha 3.15). Moreover, by forbidding others and by the word "limit" <term>kāṣṭhā</term>, it shows reverence for the subject of the Person; it shows that the flow from the beginning to the end exists for the sake of the realization of the Person—that is, "for the sake of the narrative." The meaning is that this narrative is for the sake of true knowledge <term>samyag-darśana</term>. For this narrative is taught precisely for the sake of true knowledge, and not that the narrative itself is the primary goal. (14)

**And because of the word "Self" (Atman). (15)**

This is another reason why the mention of the flow of senses and so on is for the sake of the realization of the Person. Because "This Self, hidden in all beings, does not shine forth, but is seen by the subtle, sharp intellect of those who see the subtle" (Katha 3.12), it speaks of the previously mentioned Person as the "Self." Therefore, it is understood that the others are not intended to be the "Self," and it shows that He alone is difficult to know and to be known by the refined mind. For the sake of knowing Him, it provides the narrative: "The wise person should restrain speech in the mind" (Katha 3.13). That has been explained in "Even the inferential one is in some" (Brahma Sutra 1.4.1). Thus, in many ways...

**Bhamati**
"That is the limit," so says the Veda. By the indicator of the negation of others and the indicator of the superiority of all beings, it shows that the purport is in the Person. It shows that the statement of the superiority of each subsequent one over the previous one is for that purpose, he says, "Moreover." He applies the sutra to the fact that the words beginning with 'artha' are for the sake of meditation, and the previous ones are for the sake of seeing the Person, because there is no purpose in themselves: "For the sake of the narrative" (14). "And because of the word 'Self'." Moreover, because of the consistency of the opening and the conclusion, such as "That supreme state of Vishnu, beyond the Person, there is nothing," there is a certainty of a single sentence aimed at a single Person who is the goal. Therefore, the assumption of sentence splitting or purpose splitting is not reasonable due to the fault of over-elaboration, he says, "Moreover" (15).

**Nyaya Nirnaya**
"Why?" Because the purport is the object of knowledge, and because of the lack of results in knowing the others and their superiority, he considers "because there is no purpose." How is the statement of the lack of purpose made? Doubting whether the result is established by logic, by the scripture, or by both, he rejects the first. He replies to the second: "And it is heard." Because the context is seen to be focused on the reality of the object, it is not suitable to be focused on the injunction of worship. If it is focused on the knowledge of the ultimate reality of the highest Person, then, since the doctrine of the senses is for the sake of other human goals, the focus cannot be on each individual, meaning there is no establishment of focus on each. The knowledge of the superiority of the Person is also not fruitful if it is mere inference of superiority over the senses, but why is there a causality of human purpose? He states, "However, in the Person," because of being the subject of the infinite, characterized by the absence of meaning, the desire for superiority in the Person is established by experience as having no destruction. He says, "it is seen." To one who differs in the experience of the learned regarding the fruits of seeing the superiority of the Person, he provides the Shruti: "And so." He says, "Moreover," because the entire context is focused on the knowledge of the Person. By the indicator of the negation "beyond the Person," by the word "limit" meaning boundary, and by the indicator of superiority, the Veda shows reverence for the subject of the Person. The mention of the flow from the beginning to the end is the statement of the superiority of each subsequent one over the previous one. Because there is no injunction of meditation here, how is the knowledge of the supreme Person for the sake of meditation heard? Doubting this, he explains the part of the sutra: "For the sake of the narrative." Even the knowledge of the unqualified Brahman is for the sake of meditation because it is situated in Brahman. He objects to the contradiction with the Shruti "Then, that," and says, "true knowledge" (14). He gives another reason for the Person being the one taught as superior to all: "And because of the word 'Self'." He explains the word "ca" in the sutra: "And from this also." Clarifying that, he parses the word "Atman": "That which..." He prevents the doubt that the non-shining of the Self is natural: "But is seen." He says "the mentioned," because of the "Atman" in that very Shruti. He states the intended meaning by explaining the word in the sutra: "Therefore." He states the means for the remaining previous purpose: "Of that." He states the purport of the latter part: "Refined..." He states another reason indicated by the word "ca": "That." He objects that only the regulation of speech and so on is implied in the mantra, not the injunction of meditation, and says, "That has been explained." Because the unknown meaning is for the sake of the repetition, the difficulty of knowing the Self is explained in the scripture, and because the others are easy to understand, the statement of their superiority is also meant for the purport. Thus, the opening and conclusion...

<summary>This page continues the commentary on the Brahma Sutras, focusing on whether descriptions of superiority are applied to each individual object mentioned or specifically to the Supreme Person. Adi Shankara and the sub-commentaries argue that the narrative serves the purpose of realizing the Supreme Person as the ultimate goal, rather than treating each intermediate description as a separate, primary teaching.</summary>
